Best,
Jade

Sam,

Option: move the interior restaurant scene off-location and build it on our stage. This saves us $2,000 in location fees but adds about $700 in set-build costs and requires one extra prep day. Net saving is $1,300, but we push our schedule by 24 hours on prep.

Decision needed soon so I can tell production whether to book the location or start set construction.

Thanks,
Jade

task_instruction: Advise on actor blocking and physical comedy beats for a specific sequence.
task_details: The kitchen sequence (pages 12–15) has physical comedy involving a slippery rice bag and a chair. Suggest specific, simple blocking so laughs land, note safety, and indicate where to keep beats short to preserve rhythm.
personalized:
Physical comedy note for the kitchen sequence (pgs 12–15).

Keep the blocking simple: Mina trips on the rice bag, a quick tumble into the chair, then an immediate beat of silence before the punchline. Don't add extra flailing — fast, precise physicality is funnier than messy chaos.

Safety: let's stage the tumble to look real but keep a clear landing and props that won't break. Recommend rehearsing slowly, then speeding up.

Beat timing: the pause after the fall should be one second — enough to register, not enough to lose laughter. Then deliver the line.

If anyone wants, I can block it with the actors at the next run-through (10 minutes) so it's repeatable and safe.

Subject: Two-sentence logline — quick impression? 

Hi Professor Chen,

Sorry for the late ping — I have an industry mixer tonight and wanted a quick take on this two-sentence logline: Myung runs her late eomma’s banchan shop while accidentally counseling the neighborhood’s dating life, but when a corporate chain threatens the block, she has to choose between tradition and reinvention. Thanks so much,
Jade

Dear [Recipient's Name],

Best regards,

[Your Name]

task_instruction: Advise on single-camera tone consistency and visual beats.
task_details: Student's script flips between grounded and broad comedic styles. Explain how to pick a tonal anchor and adjust visual beats to support it. Offer a sample rewrite instruction for a scene to match a more grounded, character-driven tone.
personalized:
You're oscillating between grounded sitcom and broad sketchy bits. That's okay in drafts, but you need a tonal anchor before the next pass. Decide whether this is single-camera, character-driven comedy or heightened, gag-first humor, and shape your visual beats to support that choice.

If you want the grounded approach, pull back on cartoonish cutaways and let camera choices deepen the jokes. For example, change your 'spaghetti explosion' scene from a physical gag to a cringe close-up of sauce slowly dripping down the protagonist's chin. Keep the humor in the camera's mercy, not in slapstick.

Pick the tone, then go through the script: if a beat feels louder than the anchor, tighten it or rewrite it to be quieter. Resubmit the scene reflecting your chosen tone by Thursday.

Tone is a promise to the audience. Make it and keep it. — Jade

Specificity is the dirt that grows jokes. You don't need a lecture on culture — just small, precise details that anchor a moment and invite humor.

Add a single sensory detail: the metallic clack of chopsticks, the way eomma hums when she seasons kimchi, or the leftover scent of doenjang in a bag. Add a family line that communicates history: 'You still owe me for your college tuition in jang.' And a culinary detail can be a running visual gag: the protagonist always refuses the fish sauce but pockets banchan when eomma isn't looking.

Try this line in your scene: 'Don't act surprised, you left your kimchi jar in my car and it claimed it as property.' It lands texture and a laugh.

Don't overexplain. Let the small, lived-in moments do the work. — Jade

task_instruction: Move the inciting incident later to allow more set-up of the A-story.
task_details: Episode 3, single-camera. Current draft has the inciting incident (protagonist's coffee-shop breakup) on page 4, which undermines the A-story stakes because we haven't established why this relationship mattered. Propose moving the breakup to page 12 and adding two short scenes to deepen the relationship context (a montage at the top and a mid-scene showing their domestic rhythm). Keep runtime the same; preserve existing B-story about roommate's job interview.
personalized:
Hey Sam,

Quick thought after last night's notes pass: move the inciting incident (the coffee-shop breakup) from page 4 to page 12. Right now we throw the breakup at us before the audience knows why it hurts — feels like a punchline with no setup. If we delay it, we get an A-story that lands emotionally (and gives the lead agency instead of flailing).

Concretely: open with a short montage establishing the couple's domestic rhythm (two scenes, three jokes, 60–90 seconds). Then let the initial scenes build expectation and small stakes. Drop the breakup at ~p12 as the true inciting incident. This creates space for the B-story (roommate's job interview) to breathe and not feel like filler between beats.

Why I like it: actor gets set-up to sell the hurt (better reaction shots), laugh-to-heart ratio improves, and the tag can punch with a callback to the montage. (Also, I can justify a visual gag in the cold open now.)

If you like it, I'll draft the new outline by Friday and re-block the table read pages for pacing notes. Approve to ship the rewrite?

— Jade

Jade

Subject: Decision Needed: Renting a Second Camera for B-Story Coverage

Dear Sam,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to follow up on our previous discussion regarding the B-story coverage for our upcoming project. As we continue to refine the shot list, I strongly believe that having a second camera would significantly improve our coverage options and provide us with more flexibility in terms of storytelling.

To move forward, I've outlined three options for your consideration:

Option 1: Rent a second camera for the full day at $1,200. This would provide us with the most comprehensive coverage and allow us to capture all the necessary shots without any limitations.

Option 2: Do not add a second camera, which would require us to simplify the blocking and accept fewer coverage options. This could lead to an increased likelihood of pickups and potentially cost more in reshoot time.

Option 3: Rent a second camera for a half-day at $600, specifically to capture the crucial Tuesday block. This would save us $600 compared to the full-day rental and provide us with the needed coverage for the story transition beat.

I would greatly appreciate it if you could make a decision on this matter by midday tomorrow so that we can lock in the vendor and adjust the shot list
